description: Company-level (organisation-wide) applicability rules for the SME onboarding flow. Each rule maps declared business facts to a framework exposure with an explicit confidence and a citation to the framework's own scope/applicability provision. Rules NEVER assert legal certainty where scope depends on interpretation - those resolve to LEGAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED confidence. This file is versioned data, not code: correcting a trigger means editing here and bumping ruleset_version; every ApplicabilityDecision stores which rule_ids and which ruleset_version produced it.

DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE.label: Directly applicable
DIRECTLY_APPLICABLE.meaning: The framework's own scope provision appears to cover this organisation on the declared facts.

POTENTIALLY_APPLICABLE.label: Potentially applicable
POTENTIALLY_APPLICABLE.meaning: Scope may be met depending on thresholds or facts not yet confirmed.

SUPPLY_CHAIN_INDIRECT.label: Indirect / supply-chain
SUPPLY_CHAIN_INDIRECT.meaning: Not directly in scope, but obligations flow down via enterprise customers who are in scope.

CONTRACTUALLY_REQUIRED.label: Customer / contract required
CONTRACTUALLY_REQUIRED.meaning: Commonly demanded in enterprise procurement and security reviews for this profile.

RECOMMENDED_BEST_PRACTICE.label: Recommended best practice
RECOMMENDED_BEST_PRACTICE.meaning: Voluntary framework widely treated as the standard of care for this technology.

NOT_APPLICABLE.label: Not applicable
NOT_APPLICABLE.meaning: No declared fact triggers this framework's scope.

rules.source_reference: Art. 2(1)(a) and Art. 3(3) - applies to providers placing AI systems on the EU market or putting them into service in the EU, irrespective of establishment.
rules.reasoning_template: You develop AI products and operate in / market to the EU, so the AI Act's provider obligations apply to systems you place on the EU market. The exact obligations depend on each system's risk classification (assessed per-system in Intake).

rules.source_reference: Art. 3(4) and Art. 26 - 'deployer' obligations apply to those using an AI system under their authority in the EU (lighter than provider obligations; most weight falls on high-risk uses).
rules.reasoning_template: You use AI systems internally within the EU. Deployer obligations are limited unless a system is high-risk (e.g. used for recruitment or credit decisions).

rules.source_reference: Annex III points 1, 3, 4, 5 - AI used for biometric identification, education, employment, or access to essential services is high-risk; obligations in Arts. 8-27.
rules.reasoning_template: Your AI makes decisions about people in a domain listed in Annex III ({decision_domains}). If those systems are offered or used in the EU they are likely high-risk, triggering the full Art. 8-27 obligation set. A legal review should confirm the Annex III classification and any Art. 6(3) exemption.

rules.source_reference: Art. 3 - territorial scope: applies to processing in the context of an EU establishment, or offering goods/services to, or monitoring, data subjects in the EU.
rules.reasoning_template: You handle personal data and have EU exposure (operations and/or enterprise customers with EU data subjects). GDPR applies to that processing. When AI is involved, Art. 22 (automated decisions) and Art. 35 (DPIA) may add obligations.

rules.framework_name: India Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 + DPDP Rules 2025
rules.source_reference: DPDP Act 2023 s.3 - applies to processing of digital personal data within India, and to processing outside India connected with offering goods/services to Data Principals in India.
rules.reasoning_template: You operate in or are headquartered in India and process personal data, so you are a Data Fiduciary (or Processor) under the DPDP Act. The DPDP Rules 2025 add notice, consent-manager, security-safeguard and breach-notification detail; effective dates are phased.

rules.source_reference: Art. 2 - applies to 'products with digital elements' made available on the EU market whose intended/foreseeable use includes a data connection. Pure SaaS (software as a service) is generally out of direct scope.
rules.reasoning_template: You place software or connected products (not delivered purely as SaaS) on the EU market, which is the CRA's scope. Manufacturer obligations include secure development, vulnerability handling, a support period, and incident/vulnerability reporting to ENISA. A legal review should confirm the product qualifies and its risk class.

rules.source_reference: Recital 12 / Art. 2 - software provided as a service is covered by NIS2, not the CRA, unless it is part of a product with digital elements.
rules.reasoning_template: Your product is delivered as SaaS, which is generally outside the CRA's direct scope. However, enterprise customers who ship CRA-regulated products may pass secure-development and vulnerability-handling expectations to you contractually.

rules.source_reference: Art. 21(2)(d) - in-scope essential/important entities must manage supply-chain security, including the security of their direct suppliers. Direct scope requires being an entity in an Annex I/II sector meeting size thresholds (Art. 2, Art. 3).
rules.reasoning_template: You may not meet NIS2's direct entity scope, but you sell software/services to EU enterprises that do. Those customers are required to impose supply-chain security requirements on you (Art. 21(2)(d)), so NIS2-aligned controls will appear in their security reviews.

rules.source_reference: Annex I point 8 (managed service providers / managed security service providers) + Art. 2(1) size threshold.
rules.reasoning_template: As a cybersecurity product company operating in the EU above the size threshold, you may fall within NIS2's 'digital infrastructure' or 'managed security service provider' categories as an important entity. A legal review of your specific activities and national transposition is needed.

rules.source_reference: Art. 2 - applies to a closed list of regulated 'financial entities' (credit institutions, payment institutions, investment firms, insurers, crypto-asset service providers, etc.).
rules.reasoning_template: You are in fintech and operate in the EU. DORA applies only if you are one of the regulated financial-entity types in Art. 2 - not to every fintech. If you hold or are pursuing a licence (EMI, PI, investment firm, CASP), DORA's ICT risk, incident, resilience-testing and third-party-risk obligations apply.

rules.source_reference: Art. 28-30 - financial entities must manage ICT third-party risk and include prescribed contractual terms with ICT service providers; Art. 31 designates 'critical ICT third-party providers' for direct oversight.
rules.reasoning_template: You sell SaaS to financial institutions. They are required by DORA to flow specific contractual, audit, exit-strategy and sub-outsourcing terms down to you, and to include you in their register of information. Expect DORA-shaped clauses in their contracts and security reviews.

rules.framework_name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1)
rules.source_reference: NIST AI 100-1 s.1 - 'a voluntary framework'. Not law. Widely referenced in US enterprise procurement and by the EU AI Act's harmonised-standards work.
rules.reasoning_template: You build or use AI. NIST AI RMF (GOVERN / MAP / MEASURE / MANAGE) is the most widely accepted voluntary baseline for AI governance and is frequently cited in enterprise AI questionnaires. It is not a legal requirement.

rules.source_reference: NIST AI 600-1 - a companion profile to the AI RMF for generative AI risks; voluntary.
rules.reasoning_template: You use generative AI / RAG. The NIST GenAI Profile enumerates GenAI-specific risks (confabulation, data leakage, harmful content, IP) and suggested actions on top of the AI RMF.

rules.source_reference: OWASP GenAI Security Project - community security guidance. Not law.
rules.reasoning_template: You build LLM/GenAI features. The OWASP LLM Top 10 (prompt injection, sensitive-information disclosure, supply chain, etc.) is the de-facto security checklist enterprise security teams use to review AI products.

rules.source_reference: OWASP GenAI Security Project - agentic security guidance. Not law.
rules.reasoning_template: You build AI agents. OWASP Agentic (excessive agency, tool misuse, memory poisoning, agent-to-agent risk) plus MITRE ATLAS are the reference points for agent security reviews and should drive your Agent Registry controls.

rules.framework_name: MITRE ATLAS (Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems)
rules.source_reference: MITRE ATLAS - a knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques against AI systems. It is not a regulation, framework of obligations, or certification.
rules.reasoning_template: ATLAS is a threat knowledge base (not a law or framework of obligations). Use it for AI threat modelling, red-teaming and mapping attacks to your controls.

rules.source_reference: NIST CSF 2.0 - voluntary. GOVERN / IDENTIFY / PROTECT / DETECT / RESPOND / RECOVER.
rules.reasoning_template: CSF 2.0 is the common language for describing your overall cybersecurity posture in enterprise reviews. Voluntary, but expected.

rules.jurisdiction: United States (voluntary; mandatory for US federal software suppliers)
rules.source_reference: NIST SP 800-218 - voluntary generally; required for suppliers to the US federal government under OMB M-22-18 / the secure-software self-attestation.
rules.reasoning_template: SSDF (PO/PS/PW/RV practices) is the secure-development baseline. It becomes mandatory if you sell software to the US federal government (self-attestation).

rules.framework_name: NIST SP 800-218A (SSDF augmentations for AI models)
rules.source_reference: NIST SP 800-218A - community profile augmenting the SSDF for AI/ML model development. Voluntary.
rules.reasoning_template: 800-218A extends the SSDF with AI-model-specific practices (training-data provenance, model evaluation, model supply chain). Relevant because you develop AI. (Content pending import in this platform - see framework status.)

rules.framework_name: UK AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
rules.source_reference: UK DSIT AI Cyber Security Code of Practice (2025) - a voluntary code, intended to inform a future global standard.
rules.reasoning_template: You develop AI and operate in the UK. The DSIT AI Cyber Security Code is voluntary but is the UK government's stated expectation for AI security across the lifecycle.

rules.source_reference: AI Verify Foundation - a voluntary AI governance testing framework and toolkit. Not a mandatory regulation.
rules.reasoning_template: You develop AI and operate in Singapore. AI Verify is a voluntary testing framework; adopting it signals responsible-AI maturity to Singapore-based enterprise and government buyers.

rules.jurisdiction: United States (mandatory for US federal systems; widely used as a control catalogue)
rules.source_reference: NIST SP 800-53 - mandated for US federal information systems (FISMA); the control basis for FedRAMP.
rules.reasoning_template: You sell to government / pursue FedRAMP. 800-53 is the underlying control catalogue you will be assessed against.

rules.jurisdiction: United States (voluntary; mandatory for US federal supply chains)
rules.source_reference: NIST SP 800-161r1 - Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management practices. Voluntary generally.
rules.reasoning_template: You depend on third-party AI models and sell to enterprises. C-SCRM practices (supplier assessment, provenance, SBOM-style component tracking) are increasingly required in enterprise vendor reviews. (Content pending import in this platform.)

rules.jurisdiction: United States (AICPA attestation; global market expectation)
rules.source_reference: AICPA SSAE 18 / Trust Services Criteria. A voluntary attestation, not a law - but the default entry ticket for enterprise SaaS procurement in North America.
rules.reasoning_template: You sell SaaS to enterprises. SOC 2 (Security, and often Availability/Confidentiality) is almost always requested in enterprise procurement. It is a paid third-party attestation, not a regulation. This platform maps SOC 2 criteria to your unified controls but does not reproduce AICPA copyrighted material.

rules.source_reference: ISO/IEC 27001:2022. A voluntary certification, not a law. Commonly required by enterprise buyers outside North America.
rules.reasoning_template: You sell to enterprises in markets where ISO 27001 is the expected security credential (EU, UK, India, Singapore, APAC). It is a paid accredited certification. This platform provides ISO 27001 control mappings and an evidence structure; ISO's copyrighted standard text is NOT stored - you load your licensed copy if needed.

rules.source_reference: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 - the first certifiable AI management-system standard. Voluntary.
rules.reasoning_template: You develop AI products. ISO 42001 is emerging as the AI-governance equivalent of ISO 27001 and is starting to appear in enterprise AI questionnaires. Paid certification; standard text not stored here - mappings and structure only.
